articles.title: A weekly edition, starting small
body: The Mallacoota Mouth stopped, and nothing took its place. This is a first attempt at something weekly again â smaller, and put together differently.

Approved contributors will be able to submit directly, under the headings the Mouth used. What arrives by the end of the week becomes that week's edition, and a printable copy with a table of contents.
It starts with almost nothing in it. That is the honest place to start.

articles.title: Old Mouth editions wanted
body: Thirty-seven issues are catalogued so far, covering 2020 to 2023. Issues 1772 to 1791, 1812 to 1820, and 1835 are missing, along with everything before 1771 and after 1837.
If you have old editions, or know who holds a larger collection, please get in touch through the archive page.

articles.title: From the mud of the Barwon to the quiet of Mallacoota: Frank Stokesâ deep-water days

subject.name: Frank Stokes
subject.note: Frank supplied the source material for this story and agreed to it being published.

audio.title: Listen to Frank Stokes' deep-water story

body: Long-time Mallacoota local Frank Stokes, now 87 and enjoying a well-earned retirement in town, has plenty of stories â but not everyone knows about his high-stakes days as a commercial diver helping build Victoriaâs early communications backbone.

Before tackling the treacherous coastal estuaries, Frankâs underwater skills were already well proven closer to home in East Gippsland, where he suited up to lay the critical PMG telephone cable crossing beneath the swift currents of the Snowy River at Orbost.

By late summer 1968, Frank â then 29 â took that hard-won river experience to an even bigger challenge: joining an elite eight-man crew from the Postmaster-Generalâs Department Mechanical Aids division for a pioneering engineering feat across the Barwon River to connect Barwon Heads and Ocean Grove.

Billed at the time as a first of its kind in the state, the Barwon project required laying more than 2,000 yards of four-inch polythene piping into a four-foot trench dug directly into the riverbed. While heavy machinery, bulldozers and an ex-US Marines amphibious âBuffaloâ landing craft tackled the surface, Frank geared up with his aqualung to handle the critical inspections in the murky depths below.

Working underwater meant battling thick, vile-smelling black mud, zero visibility, and brutal tidal swings fluctuating up to nine feet between low and flood tides. Excavations could only happen during narrow windows at the dead low ebb. Submerged in the channel, Frank guided the sinking pipe sections â flooded with water, weighted down with heavy-duty chains, and welded together on the surface â ensuring the conduit settled cleanly into the river floor.
On the surface, the crew contended with snakes and rats in the mangrove swamps, but beneath the waterline it came down to Frankâs nerve and skill to make sure the 99-year-guaranteed pipe sat true.

The successful crossings at both the Snowy and the Barwon paved the way for modern automatic telephone exchanges across regional Victoria. The next time you run into Frank around Mallacoota, ask him about diving the Snowy or the Barwon back in the day â just be prepared to hear how tough underwater line-laying used to be.

articles.title: Contributors: a little formatting is now allowed
body: Text submitted to the edition stays plain by default, but four things now render: **bold**, *italic*, [links](https://lovemallacoota.au/archive.html), and bullet lists.

- Start a line with a dash for a bullet
- Leave a blank line between paragraphs
- Anything else, including HTML, appears exactly as typed
That last rule is the point. A pasted <script> tag or an onclick attribute is shown as text rather than run, so a contributor cannot change how the page behaves.

articles.title: Family notices
body: Notices are published as the family sends them. There is no charge, and there never will be.

To place one, use the submission form or speak to us directly. We will not print a name until someone in the family has asked us to, and every notice needs a contact we can reach in case we have a question.

articles.title: Ninety years, and about seventy people to mark it

subject.name: Shirley Dixon
subject.note: Written and published by her son. The family supplied the photographs.

body: Around seventy locals, friends and family gathered at Karbeethong Lodge on 25 July for Shirley's ninetieth birthday.

It was an afternoon of the ordinary and best kind â people who have known each other a long time, in a room with a view of the lake, catching up and telling stories. Ninety years is a long time to be part of a place, and a good many of the people there were in the stories being told.
The afternoon's standout was an original birthday song, written and produced for Shirley by her son Colin. It raised smiles and a few tears, which is about the right response.
You can [listen to the birthday song on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wITs63Cx9AQ), and there is a [gallery of the afternoon](https://celebrate.oze.au/shirley90/) with pictures of the day.
Happy ninetieth, Shirley â from all of us.

articles.title: MADRA is asking what local information the district actually needs
body: MADRA, with support from Australian Business Volunteers, is asking Mallacoota and district what kind of trusted local information service would be most useful now that *The Mallacoota Mouth* has closed.

The survey covers local news, notices, events, community groups, school and youth activities, local history, business information, and community or emergency information. It takes about five minutes. [Take the community survey](https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/5KWFLG8) â responses close on Wednesday 9 September.
Prefer paper? Copies are at Council's Information Centre, and completed surveys go in the MADRA suggestion box there.

A word about where I stand. I have been building this weekly for a while now, so I am hardly a neutral party in a survey about what should replace the Mouth. That is exactly why it is worth filling in: if what the district wants is not what I have built, I would rather find out from a few hundred answers than from my own assumptions. Say what you actually want. I will publish what the survey finds either way.
MADRA · madrecovery.com

articles.title: Two and a half million views: what Mallacoota Now says about who is watching

check.note: Written by the publisher, who runs the group.

body: [Mallacoota Now](https://www.facebook.com/groups/mallacootanow) is where a good deal of this town's conversation happens. The group's own numbers for the eleven months to 28 August are worth putting somewhere they can be read without logging in.

- **2,664,676 views** â a median of about 3,600 a day
- **1,475 posts** and **8,083 comments**
- **63,527 reactions**
- **784 people joined** over the period, 61 of them in the last four weeks
- About **6,900 members**, across **47 countries**

The number that says the most is not the big one. Melbourne is the largest single group of members at **2,609**. Mallacoota itself accounts for **152**. Bairnsdale, Sydney, Canberra and Lakes Entrance follow.

So this is a group about Mallacoota that is mostly read somewhere else â by people who own a shack here, grew up here, holiday here, or are planning to. That is worth knowing when you post: the audience is far wider than the people you would run into at the shop, and much of it is deciding whether to come.

**What the group is for.** Nature, wildlife, weather, fires, tides and daily life. Open to everyone â locals, visitors, part-timers, and people who simply love the place. Different views are welcome; personal attacks are not.

**It is a public group.** Anything posted there is public. Images and text can be seen and shared outside the group, and permission is not required to do so. That is worth understanding before you post a photograph of someone.

**Posts go straight up.** It is not moderated in any real sense. A few automatic rules do the work: a profile photo is required, comments need at least ten characters, and Facebook's banned-words list is on. Your first post may be checked; after that it publishes itself.

**A tip that improves almost any post:** say when it was taken, where, who or what is in it, and why you shared it. One or two lines is enough, and context is what starts a conversation rather than a row of likes.
Hashtag is #MallacootaNow. Longer pieces and the weekly edition are here at [coota.au](https://coota.au).

articles.title: The Bar

audio.title: Listen to 'The Bar' by Henry Lawson

image.alt: Historic photograph of Mallacoota Bar, May 1910
image.note: Mallacoota Bar entrance, which inspired Henry Lawson during his 1910 stay

body:
We kedged her back and we poled her back
In time for the ebbing tide,
For the sky was grey and the rocks were black
And the rollers broke outside,
And its O My Love but the lines are slack,
And the weary world is wide.

We'd try to get over the Bar tonight,
Tonight on the highest tide;
But the moon is dull that last night was bright
And the world is dark outside,
O Love.. New Love!.. is your face so white,
And the weary world so wide?

We tried to get over the bar today,
Tomorrow we'll try again.
Oh Love!.. New Love of the grey eyes, say
Is the strife of man in vain?
The glass might lie, and the needle stray,
But the path of love is plain!

When over the Bar, there is no return
In the time of the Autumn gales..
But whether the sea or the Bush it be,
The heart of a man prevails..
O Love! New Love, you may watch the sea
Where the Bushman sailor sails!

articles.title: Bringing Mallacoota’s Literary History to Life: Henry Lawson, E.J. Brady, and the Family Behind the Camp

audio.title: Listen to the Henry Lawson & E.J. Brady story

images.alt: 1910 meeting on Captain’s Point between bush poet Henry Lawson and E.J. Brady
images.note: 1910 meeting on Captain’s Point between bush poet Henry Lawson and his close friend, writer and bush advocate Edwin James (E.J.) Brady.

body: The restoration and colorisation of early Mallacoota photographs offer a vivid window into Australia’s frontier literary era. Among the most iconic scenes is the 1910 meeting on Captain’s Point between bush poet Henry Lawson and his close friend, writer and bush advocate Edwin James (E.J.) Brady.

A closer look at the historic photograph reveals subtle details easily missed in grainy black-and-white archives. In the background behind Lawson and Brady, a child can be seen playfully sliding down the canvas tent. Family records clarify that this young girl was Brady’s daughter, fondly known as "Tuppy". Years later during the Great Depression, Tuppy—remembered as a spirited socialist with a sharp wit—helped run Mallacoota House alongside her husband.

Tuppy’s mother, Norma, was central to life at Captain’s Point. Described by visitors such as author Katharine Susannah Prichard as a steadfast "Juno of a woman," Norma managed the bush camp and raised a growing family during Brady’s extended absences in the city. Archival portraits of Norma in elegant period dress and later images of E.J. Brady in his flourishing Mallacoota flower garden provide authentic references for restoring these snapshots of early coastal life.

When Henry Lawson arrived in Mallacoota in February 1910 to rest and recover, he fell in love with the remote wilderness and its working folk. His time camped with the Bradys inspired classic poems such as Captain’s Point, The Bar, and Mallacoota West. By restoring these images in full color—from the bush workwear to the casual moments caught around the campsite—the human stories behind Mallacoota's artistic heritage remain just as vibrant today.
